newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul minister sees N.Korea surviving food crisis.
newsitem.headline: Seoul minister sees N.Korea surviving food crisis.

text.p: Famine-threatened North Korea will be able to survive until the next harvest if international food aid flows smoothly, South Korea's Minister of National Unification said on Friday.

"If outside food shipments such as those by us and the international community go smoothly, we assume North Korea will be able to get through this year's food crisis," Kwon O-kie told a presidential advisory body.
Its own food production, supplemented by overseas aid already delivered or in the pipeline, would stave off famine until the next grain harvest starting in August, he said.
On Monday, South Korea's Red Cross signed an agreement with its Northern counterpart to deliver 50,000 tonnes of food, most of it corn.

The European Union last week pledged 155,000 tonnes of relief, including 65,000 tonnes to a World Food Programme (WFP) appeal for 200,000 tonnes of food worth $98.5 million. The United States has pledged $25 million to the WFP appeal and the South Korean government $16 million.
China has pledged an additional 70,000 tonnes of food.
The WFP estimates that 1.3 million tonnes of food is needed to head off starvation among 4.7 million North Koreans, about a fifth of the population.
Kwon said the North's economic crisis had opened cracks in the reclusive state's political system and society, highlighted by an increasing number of defectors.
Since North Korea's "Great Leader" Kim Il-sung died in 1994 some 40 to 50 defectors had taken asylum in the South each year compared with six to seven in the 1980s.
"This year, the number stands at 46, including five who arrived yesterday, and it is expected to reach 100 by the end of the year," Kwon said.

The five who landed at Seoul's international airport on Thursday from an unidentified third country included the mother, a younger sister and a younger brother of a defector who arrived last year, and who is now a student at Korea University.
However, Kwon said Seoul believed that Pyongyang leader Kim Jong-il was still in full control of the military.
"The government's judgment is that Kim Jong-il is currently in a full control of the military and, accordingly, North Korea is in a stable situation politically," Kwon said.
He said there was no evidence to support contentions that Kim Jong-il would assume top positions left vacant by the death of his father after the third anniversary of Kim Il-sung's passing on July 8.
The younger Kim has yet to assume the titles of state president and general secretary of the ruling Workers' Party, but he is Supreme Commander of the military.
Severe floods destroyed food stocks and grain harvests in North Korea in 1995 and 1996, pushing the Stalinist state to the brink of famine.
South and North Korea have been technically at war since their 1950-53 conflict ended in a truce.
